paras: The threatened lynching of Oscar Franklin took place in Manhattan, New York City, on the night of 28 June 1903, when a crowd that had followed a policeman chasing Franklin, a Black waiter, yelled for him to be lynched as he was dragged from a cellar. Franklin had been accused of stabbing the hand of a Chinese restaurant keeper, Loo Sung. The officer drove the crowd back and took Franklin to the station.

Franklin, described as "a colored waiter" living at 241 West Twenty-ninth Street, entered Loo Sung's chop suey restaurant at 331 Eighth Avenue that evening with a woman companion. According to the Tribune, they quarreled over an extra knife and fork and the bill, and crockery was thrown. When Loo Sung grabbed Franklin as he left, Franklin allegedly stabbed the restaurant keeper's hand, and Loo Sung went to a window with a police whistle.

Policeman Beattie of the West Thirty-seventh Street station chased Franklin from Twenty-seventh Street down Ninth Avenue and along Twenty-sixth Street. Seeing a mob following the policeman, Franklin ran into Franklin Terrace on Twenty-sixth Street and hid in the farthest corner of a cellar. When Beattie dragged him out, the crowd met them yelling "Lynch him! String him up!"
Beattie drove back the mob, and two policemen from nearby posts helped him take Franklin to the station. No injury to Franklin is reported, and the size and makeup of the crowd are not given.
No report of a charge or court outcome for Franklin, or of arrests in the crowd, was found.

The New-York Tribune carried the only account found, a short local item on page 12 of its 29 June issue. Its headline, "Wanted to Lynch Negro," and deck, "He Stabbed Chinaman, Mob Pursued Dragged from Cellar," stated the stabbing as fact, though the body hedged it with "it is alleged" and "it is said." The story was told in a joking register, describing Franklin's Tuxedo suit, "merry mood" and ragtime singing, and it neither condemned nor endorsed the crowd's cry.
No account of the incident was found in the Black press.

bases: A crowd following a policeman's chase yelled for Franklin to be lynched and hanged once he was found, but the officer drove it back and no violence by the crowd is reported (A1); a threatened lynching.
Franklin was not killed or reported injured; a 'mob' of unstated size called for his lynching over an alleged stabbing, but Policeman Beattie drove it back and took him to the station (A1).
Only the New-York Tribune report was found; no second white or any Black-press account turned up (A1).

accounts.label: New-York Tribune local report
accounts.gist: Franklin quarreled with Loo Sung over a bill, allegedly stabbed his hand, fled, and was found in a cellar by Policeman Beattie, who drove back a mob yelling 'Lynch him!' and took him to the station.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'WANTED TO LYNCH NEGRO' and told the restaurant quarrel in a joking register, presenting the stabbing as alleged but stating 'He Stabbed Chinaman' in the deck; it neither condemned nor endorsed the mob.

record_check.dossier: The Monday 29 June paper says 'last night', which places the incident on the night of Sunday 28 June, not 27-28 June; event_date 1903-06-28 is consistent.
Black: the Tribune calls Franklin 'a colored waiter' and 'the negro'.
0: no injury to Franklin is reported.
Franklin had just been dragged from the cellar by Policeman Beattie when the mob yelled; he was in the officer's hands, at the end of a pursuit, not yet at the station.

info: Night of Sunday 28 June 1903 ('last night' in the Monday 29 June paper)
Chase from Loo Sung's restaurant, 331 Eighth Avenue, through Twenty-seventh Street and Ninth Avenue to a cellar at Franklin Terrace, West Twenty-sixth Street, Manhattan
Oscar Franklin, 'a colored waiter', of 241 West Twenty-ninth Street
Alleged ('it is said') to have stabbed the hand of Chinese restaurant keeper Loo Sung, who had grabbed him after a dispute over the bill
A 'mob' that followed the policeman in the chase; members not named or described
Beattie drove back the mob and police took Franklin to the station; no later court outcome was found
